summary: Suggests a method for personal computers and workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server, called IMAP version 2. It obsoletes RFC 1064. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Your mail stays in a big mailbox far away, and this lets your computer look at it and manage it there without bringing it all home.

questions: how does imap2 differ from pop
subtitle: Keep your mail on a server and let your PC or workstation search, read and manage it there.

tldr.problem: Personal computers and workstations are poor places to receive and keep mail: they may be busy, broken, single-tasking or not backed up.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP2 keeps the mailbox on a server. The client sends tagged commands such as SELECT, FETCH, STORE and SEARCH over a reliable stream (TCP port 143), and the server answers, also pushing unsolicited updates.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1176 is an Experimental protocol that obsoletes RFC 1064. It works as a functional superset of the Post Office Protocols and leaves sending mail to SMTP.

today: RFC 1176 is an Experimental protocol specification that obsoletes RFC 1064. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Mail Stays on a Server
sections.content:
The Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 2 (IMAP2) lets a workstation, personal computer or similar small machine access electronic mail from a mailbox server, also called a repository. The RFC lists problems with receiving mail directly on a personal machine: background tasks may not run for long periods, a hardware failure can keep a user off the air, such machines are often not backed up, addresses are hard to track when each person has a distinct machine, and keeping many different machines working with complex mailing protocols is difficult.

So the PC or workstation is called the client and should not hold the mailbox. A server holds it, can be reached from many places, and can be used by several clients at different times or even at once. IMAP2 handles reading and managing mail only; posting mail is left to a mail transfer protocol such as SMTP (RFC 821).
sections.plainLanguage: It is safer to keep your letters in one sturdy post office box than in a pocket of every coat you own.

sections.title: How IMAP2 Differs from POP and DMSP
sections.content:
The RFC calls IMAP2 a functional superset of the Post Office Protocols (POP2 and POP3, described in RFC 937 and RFC 1081). Unlike POP, it offers remote searching and parsing on the server. A free text search can run over the whole mailbox without the client transferring it. The server can also break a message into a structured envelope, so a client can show sender and subject, and implement REPLY, without parsing RFC 822 headers. It also offers per-message state and mailbox management beyond POP's simple delete.

It is also compared to the DMSP protocol of PCMAIL (RFC 1056). PCMAIL keeps long-term shared state with registered clients. In IMAP2 the client and server relationship lasts only as long as the TCP connection, all mailbox state is on the server, and the client keeps nothing between sessions. IMAP2 is primarily an online system.
sections.plainLanguage: An older way just lets you carry the whole bag of mail home. This way lets you ask the post office to find the one letter you want and tell you about it.

sections.title: Tagged Commands and Unsolicited Data
sections.content:
The protocol is a stream of client commands and server responses. Every command starts with a unique tag (for example A0001), and the server's completion response carries the same tag. Anything the server sends on its own uses the reserved tag, an asterisk, and is unsolicited data. A third reserved tag, the plus sign, tells the client that the server is ready for the text of a literal. Because a command is complete only when the matching tagged response arrives, the client does not lose synchronization, and it may send further commands without waiting. The protocol assumes a reliable stream such as TCP, where the server listens on port 143.

The server sends an OK greeting when a connection opens, and the client must not send commands before it. Normally the first command is LOGIN with a user name and password, unless identity is established another way such as Kerberos. Until then only LOGIN and LOGOUT are permitted. Then the client sends SELECT; no mailbox is selected by default, and the name INBOX must mean the user's primary mailbox. A successful SELECT returns the valid flags, the number of messages and the number of recent messages.

The client keeps a local cache of mailbox data and updates it from unsolicited data. A FETCH is a request to make sure the cache is current, and the RFC compares the model to page-fault handling on a demand-paged system.
sections.plainLanguage: Each question you ask gets a number on it, and the answer comes back with the same number. The server may also toss in extra news, like "you have new mail", without being asked.

sections.title: Commands, Flags and Envelopes
sections.content:
The commands are NOOP, LOGIN, LOGOUT, SELECT, BBOARD, FIND MAILBOXES, FIND BBOARDS, CHECK, EXPUNGE, COPY, FETCH, STORE and SEARCH. BBOARD and the two FIND commands are optional.

FETCH returns three kinds of data: per-message data (FLAGS, INTERNALDATE, RFC822.SIZE, which together are the macro FAST), the parsed ENVELOPE (ALL adds it to FAST), and text for people to read (RFC822.HEADER, RFC822.TEXT and RFC822). The envelope lists date, subject, from, sender, reply-to, to, cc, bcc, in-reply-to and message-id. Not-applicable fields are NIL, and the server defaults reply-to and sender from the from field. This is not the SMTP envelope.

The five system flags are \RECENT, \SEEN, \ANSWERED, \FLAGGED and \DELETED. STORE changes flags with FLAGS, +FLAGS or -FLAGS. Deleting a message means setting \DELETED; EXPUNGE then removes marked messages permanently and the server sends an unsolicited EXPUNGE response for each. Messages are named by a sequence such as 2,4:7,9,12:15.

SEARCH returns the messages matching all given criteria, for example SEARCH DELETED FROM "SMITH" SINCE 1-OCT-87. String matches are case-independent substring matches, and criteria include TO, CC, SUBJECT, BODY, TEXT, BEFORE, ON, SINCE, NEW, OLD and flag tests such as SEEN and UNSEEN.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands are like asking a librarian to list the books, read one aloud, put a sticker on one, or hunt for every book with a certain word in it.

sections.title: A Typical Session
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a session. The client logs in, selects INBOX and receives the flag list plus counts (19 messages exist and 2 are recent in its example). It fetches ALL for messages 1 to 19 to build a menu, then fetches RFC822.TEXT for message 8 to read it. A STORE with +Flags \Deleted marks it, EXPUNGE removes it, and LOGOUT makes the server send BYE followed by an OK.

The responses are OK (success), NO (the command failed, and the text should be shown to the user) and BAD (faulty protocol from the client). The untagged BYE announces that the server is closing the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: You walk in, show your key, open your box, look at the labels on all the letters, read one, throw it away and leave.

sections.title: Implementation Status and Limits
sections.content:
The memo reports operational software from the University of Washington (a client library called the C-Client, and clients for BSD Unix and the NeXT) and from Stanford University/SUMEX (clients for Xerox Lisp machines, Texas Instruments Explorers and the Apple Macintosh, and servers for TOPS-20 and BSD Unix). It notes NTT also built a client.

The specification sets no formal size limits, but the DEC-20 server has some, such as a mailbox length of 7,077,888 characters, at most 18,432 messages and a command line of 10,000 characters. The RFC says that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Several schools built working versions, and the one big server they describe has a limit on how many letters one box can hold.
